recipes.title: Prepare installation and recovery USB media
recipes.description: Choose by the machine preparing the drive, the image type and whether one drive must hold several installers. These are documented workflow fits; no firmware compatibility or write-speed comparison was performed.

picks.label: Windows host with boot-setting controls
picks.reason: Use when a Windows PC needs to prepare installation media with explicit BIOS/UEFI and image options.
picks.tradeoff: Writing erases the selected destination; the image and target hardware still need compatibility checks.

picks.label: Several boot images on one drive
picks.reason: Use when maintaining a portable library of installers or rescue images that can be copied onto a prepared drive.
picks.tradeoff: Initial preparation reformats the drive; image, Secure Boot and firmware behavior varies.

picks.label: Straightforward image flashing across desktop systems
picks.reason: Use when the main task is writing and validating an existing disk image on Windows, macOS or Linux.
picks.tradeoff: It is an image writer; advanced installer customization and multi-image boot menus require other tools.

picks.label: Raspberry Pi setup
picks.reason: Use when selecting a Raspberry Pi operating system and preparing its storage through the official setup workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Its configuration options serve Raspberry Pi deployment rather than every PC installer.

recipes.title: Choose a partition-management workflow
recipes.description: Separate offline partition layout work, everyday Linux disk administration and a combined Windows disk utility. Backups and a verified destination matter because these operations change stored data.

picks.label: Offline layout changes
picks.reason: Use GParted Live to work on supported filesystems without keeping the installed operating system running.
picks.tradeoff: Operation support varies by filesystem; interruption, wrong-device selection or unsupported resize conditions can lose data.

picks.label: Routine Linux device administration
picks.reason: Use within GNOME to inspect devices, configure volumes and work with disk images.
picks.tradeoff: It is tied to the Linux storage stack, and formatting changes the selected device.

picks.label: Combined Windows disk workflow
picks.reason: Use when partition management, cloning and recovery inspection are needed in one Windows application.
picks.tradeoff: Free and Professional features differ; exact EULA and recovery outcomes still need independent assessment.

recipes.title: Send files without setting up continuous synchronization
recipes.description: Pick according to whether devices are nearby, recipients prefer a browser, both parties can run a terminal tool or a Tor-based sharing route is needed.

picks.label: Nearby devices with an app
picks.reason: Use for local-network transfers across supported devices through a dedicated sharing interface.
picks.tradeoff: Devices need local reachability and the app; discovery can be affected by network isolation.

picks.label: Browser-based peer exchange
picks.reason: Use when recipients can open a browser and establish a supported WebRTC connection.
picks.tradeoff: Signaling, relay and browser/network behavior affect connectivity; current maintenance is unverified in this review.

picks.label: Command-line transfer with a short code
picks.reason: Use when both endpoints can run a CLI and transfer through its direct or relay-assisted workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Share the code through an appropriate channel; relay availability and endpoint/network conditions still matter.

picks.label: Sharing through a Tor onion service
picks.reason: Use when the sender wants the sharing endpoint reached through Tor rather than a conventional public file-hosting URL.
picks.tradeoff: Recipients generally need a Tor-capable client, and throughput and connection behavior differ from local sharing.

recipes.title: Choose a local DNS role
recipes.description: DNS filtering, authoritative zones and recursive resolution solve different parts of name resolution. Choose the role before choosing the server, and keep a recovery path for network DNS settings.

picks.label: Network-wide filtering with encrypted upstreams
picks.reason: Use for a local DNS filtering service with a web interface and upstream configuration.
picks.tradeoff: Filtering only sees DNS paths that use the service; devices with independent encrypted DNS can bypass the intended policy.

picks.label: Linux DNS filtering appliance
picks.reason: Use when a Linux or Raspberry Pi service should provide network-wide DNS blocklists and administration.
picks.tradeoff: It does not remove every advertisement and requires correct client/router DNS settings.

picks.label: Authoritative zones and advanced DNS administration
picks.reason: Use when managing local authoritative zones, recursive service and DNS features through one server UI.
picks.tradeoff: The wider server feature set requires DNS knowledge and careful exposure/recursion settings.

picks.label: Validating recursive resolver
picks.reason: Use when the requirement is DNSSEC-validating recursive resolution rather than an advertisement-filtering dashboard.
picks.tradeoff: It needs resolver configuration; filtering lists, client policy and GUI administration are separate concerns.

recipes.title: Measure a local network path
recipes.description: Place a test server on the network path being investigated so internet access is not the only measured path. These products run different tests; this guide does not claim comparable benchmark scores.

picks.label: Controlled terminal-to-terminal throughput
picks.reason: Use when both endpoints can run a test process and you need explicit transfer parameters.
picks.tradeoff: Results depend on endpoint CPU, direction, protocol and test settings; they are not a blanket measure of application performance.

picks.label: Browser clients against a local server
picks.reason: Use when a self-hosted speed-test endpoint should be reachable from common web browsers.
picks.tradeoff: Browser, TLS, server and device limits can affect measured throughput.

picks.label: Customizable self-hosted web speed test
picks.reason: Use when operating a web-based test with configurable server/backend deployment.
picks.tradeoff: Hosting and backend requirements add administration; internet and local deployments answer different questions.

picks.label: Latency trends alongside throughput tests
picks.reason: Use to graph repeated ping responses while investigating a particular path or load period.
picks.tradeoff: ICMP handling and rate limits can differ from real application traffic; low ping does not establish high bandwidth.

recipes.title: Monitor a personal server and its services
recipes.description: Service availability, infrastructure metrics and historical process accounting complement one another. Match the evidence collected to the question you need to answer after a problem.

picks.label: Service reachability and notifications
picks.reason: Use for service checks, status pages and notifications around endpoints you operate.
picks.tradeoff: A successful check does not prove all application functions work; monitoring from the same host can miss whole-host outages.

picks.label: Live infrastructure dashboards
picks.reason: Use for broad metrics, collectors and dashboards when detailed system telemetry is useful.
picks.tradeoff: The agent, UI and cloud have different licenses and service tiers; telemetry overhead and data exposure need deployment-specific review.

picks.label: Scriptable Linux metric history
picks.reason: Use sar/iostat and related tools for CPU, storage and system activity records.
picks.tradeoff: Collection must be enabled before historical evidence exists, and interpreting counters needs context.

picks.label: Historical Linux process resource use
picks.reason: Use when identifying processes associated with earlier resource pressure is important.
picks.tradeoff: History depends on configured collection and retention; not every incident can be reconstructed from sampled counters.

recipes.title: Understand and configure Linux laptop power use
recipes.description: Measurement, power policy and firmware updates serve different purposes. No universal battery-life improvement is promised, and hardware support varies.

picks.label: Inspect power-related activity
picks.reason: Use to investigate power consumers and review available tunables on supported Linux hardware.
picks.tradeoff: Power estimates depend on available telemetry and calibration; tuning can affect device behavior.

picks.label: Apply persistent laptop power policy
picks.reason: Use when a supported Linux laptop needs configurable AC/battery policies and hardware-dependent controls.
picks.tradeoff: Avoid conflicting power-management services; charge thresholds and other features depend on hardware/driver support.

picks.label: Check supported firmware update paths
picks.reason: Use when the device vendor distributes firmware through a supported fwupd/LVFS path.
picks.tradeoff: Only supported devices and vendor-published firmware are covered; updating firmware requires an appropriate power and recovery plan.

recipes.title: Choose a Mac Linux and container environment
recipes.description: Decide whether you mainly need container tooling, customizable Linux machines, a native integrated interface or guest desktop virtual machines.

picks.label: CLI container environment
picks.reason: Use when Docker/containerd or Kubernetes workflows should run through a configurable local VM setup.
picks.tradeoff: It relies on Lima and container tooling; some networking, architecture and storage behavior needs configuration.

picks.label: Configurable Linux machines
picks.reason: Use when defining and running Linux VMs with shared files and forwarded services is the core task.
picks.tradeoff: It is a VM foundation rather than a complete graphical desktop-management product.

picks.label: Integrated native Mac interface
picks.reason: Use when containers and Linux machines should be managed together through a native app and CLI.
picks.tradeoff: Current builds require macOS 14+; free-use eligibility is limited, and covered professional uses require a license.

picks.label: Guest desktop and architecture choices
picks.reason: Use when running guest operating systems or emulated architectures through a Mac virtual-machine UI is the priority.
picks.tradeoff: Guest graphics, architecture and acceleration support vary; it is a different workflow from a Docker-compatible container environment.

recipes.title: Choose where desktop one-time-password secrets live
recipes.description: Hardware-backed OTP storage and a synchronized authenticator offer different recovery and daily-use tradeoffs. Check account recovery options before changing authentication.

picks.label: OTP secrets on a compatible YubiKey
picks.reason: Use when OTP credentials should reside on supported hardware rather than solely in a desktop application database.
picks.tradeoff: A compatible key is required; losing it without account recovery or a separately provisioned backup can prevent sign-in.

picks.label: Dedicated authenticator across devices
picks.reason: Use when an authenticator needs encrypted synchronization, desktop/browser access or offline local use.
picks.tradeoff: Cloud synchronization and account recovery are separate choices; exported OTP secrets need protection.

picks.label: TOTP within a local password database
picks.reason: Use when an existing KeePassXC database is the intended place to manage relevant credentials and time-based codes.
picks.tradeoff: Keeping a password and its OTP secret in the same vault changes the separation between authentication factors.

recipes.title: Operate a file-exchange service
recipes.description: Choose by the protocols and administration model your users need. A persistent service requires authentication, updates, permissions and backup decisions beyond a one-time transfer.

picks.label: Managed protocol gateway with storage backends
picks.reason: Use when controlled user access should bridge SFTP/WebDAV and local or object storage.
picks.tradeoff: Community and Enterprise capabilities differ, and the web theme has separate reuse restrictions.

picks.label: Flexible browser-facing file server
picks.reason: Use when uploads, downloads and a browser file interface should be served from a configurable standalone service.
picks.tradeoff: Its many protocol and permission options require careful configuration before exposing a public endpoint.

picks.label: Existing SSH/SFTP administration
picks.reason: Use when standard SSH accounts and SFTP already fit the host and access model.
picks.tradeoff: It does not provide the same browser portal or storage-backend management as a dedicated file-exchange server.

recipes.title: Mount remote files in local workflows
recipes.description: Choose a mount by protocol, host platform and tolerance for remote-filesystem semantics. A remote mount is not a local backup and can behave differently during disconnection.

picks.label: SFTP mounts on Unix-like hosts
picks.reason: Use when an existing SSH/SFTP server should appear as a filesystem on a compatible Linux, macOS or BSD host.
picks.tradeoff: FUSE support is required; the project reports limited maintainer capacity despite release activity.

picks.label: Windows drive access through SSHFS
picks.reason: Use when a Windows workflow specifically needs the SSHFS/WinFsp integration.
picks.tradeoff: The reviewed release feed is old; verify current Windows and authentication compatibility before relying on it.

picks.label: Remote storage with many backend types
picks.reason: Use when cloud/object-storage protocols and scripted copy, sync or mount operations are needed.
picks.tradeoff: Mount behavior varies by backend and caching choices; API costs and storage-provider limits remain separate.

picks.label: Commercial desktop mounting interface
picks.reason: Use when a graphical commercial client is preferred for supported remote storage protocols.
picks.tradeoff: License cost and backend limitations apply, and remote storage is not equivalent to a fully local filesystem.

recipes.title: Add Linux server auditing and response
recipes.description: Configuration auditing, file-integrity baselines and log-based blocking are complementary controls. None of these alone establishes that a machine is uncompromised.

picks.label: Review configuration and hardening
picks.reason: Use to gather audit findings and examine configuration weaknesses on supported Unix-like systems.
picks.tradeoff: Findings require interpretation for the host role; an audit score is not proof of security.

picks.label: Detect changes from a trusted baseline
picks.reason: Use when tracking unexpected file and metadata changes against a prepared baseline is needed.
picks.tradeoff: The initial database must be trustworthy and protected; legitimate updates also change files.

picks.label: Respond to repeated log-matched attempts
picks.reason: Use when selected service logs should trigger configured temporary bans.
picks.tradeoff: Parser rules and firewall actions must fit the service; false positives can lock out legitimate users.

picks.label: Detection scenarios with separate remediation
picks.reason: Use when a scenario-based log detection engine and optional community intelligence fit the environment.
picks.tradeoff: Enforcement needs an appropriate remediation component; engine and hosted-service licensing/pricing are separate.

recipes.title: Choose control for a private overlay network
recipes.description: Distinguish a hosted coordination service, a self-hosted Tailscale control server and an independently operated certificate-based overlay. The choice changes operational responsibility.

picks.label: Managed coordination and client ecosystem
picks.reason: Use when supported clients and a hosted coordination service fit the desired administration model.
picks.tradeoff: Service tiers and control-plane dependence apply; client behavior and network policy still require configuration.

picks.label: Self-host Tailscale-compatible coordination
picks.reason: Use for a small self-hosted control plane with compatible Tailscale clients.
picks.tradeoff: It is a coordination server rather than a replacement VPN client; compatibility and supported feature scope differ from the hosted service.

picks.label: Operate a certificate-based overlay
picks.reason: Use when managing your own certificate authority, host identities and lighthouse discovery is appropriate.
picks.tradeoff: You own certificate issuance, rotation, discovery infrastructure and firewall policy.

picks.label: WireGuard mesh with managed or self-hosted control
picks.reason: Use when its administration and access-policy model matches the network and chosen hosting approach.
picks.tradeoff: Control services, identity integration and hosted-plan terms require separate deployment review.
